title: Weak Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves
short: Halfway to equivalence the pH equals the pKa, and at equivalence the pH is above 7.
trouble: Students think the equivalence point is always at pH 7.

blocks.html: Titrating a weak acid with a strong base gives a different curve from the strong–strong case. Between the start and the equivalence point the flask holds a buffer, so the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation does most of the work.

Start: weak-acid pH. Before equivalence: a buffer, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log(n_{\mathrm{A^-}}/n_\mathrm{HA})$; at the halfway point $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$. At equivalence: only $\mathrm{A^-}$, a weak base, so the pH is above 7. After: excess $\mathrm{OH^-}$ sets the pH.

Each portion of NaOH turns some HA into $\mathrm{A^-}$. Halfway, half is converted, so $n_{\mathrm{A^-}} = n_\mathrm{HA}$ and the log term is zero. That is how $\text{p}K_a$ values are measured. At equivalence every HA has become $\mathrm{A^-}$, which takes protons from water and makes $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the pH is basic. The jump at equivalence is smaller than for a strong acid, because the curve starts higher.

blocks.name: ch-titration
blocks.cap: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid with 0.100 M NaOH. At 12.5 mL (halfway) the pH equals the pKa, 4.74; the equivalence point is near pH 8.7.

blocks.title: Acetic acid with NaOH
blocks.q: $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.100\ \text{M}$ acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$) is titrated with $0.100\ \text{M}$ NaOH. Find the pH at $0$, $12.5$, $20.0$ and $25.0\ \text{mL}$.
steps: 0 mL: weak acid, $x = \sqrt{(1.8 \times 10^{-5})(0.100)} = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$; pH 2.87. (Solving exactly gives 2.88, the value on the curve above; the small-x shortcut is off by 0.01.)

blocks.title: pKa from a curve
blocks.q: In a titration of an unknown weak acid, equivalence comes at $18.0\ \text{mL}$ of base, and the pH at $9.0\ \text{mL}$ is 3.75. What is $K_a$?

blocks.html: After equivalence, the excess hydroxide sets the pH just as in the strong-acid case, so the two curves become the same from there on.

Thinking the equivalence point is always at pH 7. It is at 7 only when both acid and base are strong. With a weak acid, the conjugate base left at equivalence makes the solution basic; with a weak base titrated by a strong acid, the conjugate acid makes it acidic. Check: ask what species is in the flask at equivalence.
You can run this titration on the bench in the Mixing Lab.
